column4: The section's dictionary branch says the camel's أعطى means yielding to its rider; 36:72 says God subdued the animals for people and made some their mounts. The verse makes the animal's compliance a granted condition of riding.

The section says the docility of a mount is a blessing rather than the rider's achievement. In 43:13 the rider is to remember God's favor and say سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَٰذَا and مَا كُنَّا لَهُ مُقْرِنِينَ, naming both the gift and human inability.

The section stages a rider carried along a road by a yielding animal. 16:7 says livestock carry loads to a destination people could not reach without great hardship, making the mount's easing of the journey concrete.
The section develops a careful horse and a camel that may or may not yield to a rider; 16:8 names horses, mules, and donkeys as animals made for riding, directly extending the same riding scene.
The section treats animal docility and carriage as divine provision. 40:79 says God made livestock so that people ride some and eat others, matching the mount as a bestowed use.

The section explicitly cites Ibrahim's prayer وَٱجْنُبْنِى وَبَنِىَّ أَن نَّعْبُدَ ٱلْأَصْنَامَ and explains it through the source-section dictionary verb جنبت الدابة, leading a horse by one's side: being led aside becomes a plea for protection from idolatry.

The source-section dictionary phrase أعطى البعير names a camel's yielding; 20:50 uses أَعْطَىٰ for God's giving each thing its created form and then guiding it. That puts the mount's fitted, responsive nature under its Creator's gift and guidance.

The section links 92:11's falling to the failure of wealth to help its owner. In 69:28 the speaker says his wealth did not avail him, a direct eschatological counterpart that clarifies the limit of worldly possession at the fall.

The section pictures the most God-fearing person being led away from the Fire by another. 39:73 says those who feared their Lord are driven in groups to Paradise; the passive leading preserves the dependence on a guide while reversing the destination.
The section's وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا image keeps the most God-fearing person away from the Fire. 21:101 says those promised the best are kept far from it, giving a direct parallel to that spatial removal.

The section makes being kept away from the Fire the outcome of the guided, God-fearing person. 3:185 defines success as being moved far from the Fire and admitted to the Garden, spelling out what this avoidance means.

The source-section root و ق ي joins careful avoidance to protection; 52:18 says their Lord protected them from Hell's punishment. It gives the divine protection behind the section's image of being led away from the Fire.

The section says the most God-fearing are taken aside from the Fire. After 19:71 says everyone will approach it, 19:72 specifies that God saves the God-fearing and leaves the wrongdoers there; this row supplies the selective rescue.

The section's image is of a person riding a made-subservient animal. 43:12 names ships and riding animals among what God created; it sets up the next verse's mounting, gratitude, and acknowledgement of dependence.
The section emphasizes the rider being carried by another creature. 23:22 says people are carried both upon livestock and ships, extending that relation from the animal road to travel by sea.

The section quotes 36:71's claim that people own the livestock, then 36:72 says God subdued them for riding. This verse's own claim of ownership is bounded by the following verse's reminder that their usefulness depends on God's subduing.

The section's source dictionaries develop the yielding and untrained camel; 88:17 asks people to look at the camels and how they were created. It directs attention to the created animal whose behavior the section reads closely.

The section says the saved person cannot pull himself away from the Fire; another holds the reins. In 7:43 the people of the Garden say they would not have been guided unless God had guided them, directly expressing dependence on another's guidance.

The section describes the mount carrying its rider as a benefit not produced by the rider. 40:80 adds that people reach needs in their hearts through livestock and are carried on them and on ships, specifying the practical value of being carried.
The section frames the mount as a reminder of its Lord. 43:14 follows the riding recollection of 43:13 with the rider's return to the Lord, giving the journey an eschatological direction.
The section's rider depends on a creature to bear him along the way. 17:70 says people are carried on land and sea, extending that dependence to human travel generally.

After 39:71's disbelievers are driven to Hell, 39:72 opens its gates and names their destination as a lasting abode. That continuation completes the opposite route to the section's person being led away from the Fire.

The section's image places the God-fearing person at a distance from the Fire. 19:71 says everyone will approach it; the next ayah distinguishes those God saves, making this approach the boundary that the section's being led aside crosses.

After 21:101 says the promised people are kept far from the Fire, 21:102 adds that they will not hear even its faintest sound. The neighbour makes the section's distance from the Fire a complete safety.

The source-section root و ق ي includes avoiding harm, and 92:17 depicts the God-fearing being moved aside from the Fire. 66:6 commands believers to protect themselves and their families from it, contrasting active guarding with the section's passive rescue.

The section develops a horse that must read the ground and a mount made easy to follow; 67:15 calls the earth ذَلُولًا and tells people to walk its slopes. It moves the image of a tractable surface from the animal to the ground beneath the traveler.

The source-section root ي س ر describes an animal that is easy to follow and light in its legs. 87:8 says God will ease the addressee toward ease, preserving the section's sense that ease is made possible by another.
The source-section roots ي س ر and ع س ر distinguish the easy-following mount from the untrained camel; 94:5 states that with hardship comes ease, putting that contrast into a promise about hardship.

The same source-section contrast between the easy mount and the untrained camel is repeated in 94:6's assurance that with hardship comes ease. Its repetition reinforces the transition from difficulty to ease.

The section sets the untrained camel's resistance against the mount made easy to follow. 65:7 promises that God will bring ease after difficulty, expressing the same change of condition in a human provision context.

The source-section dictionary calls an unbroken camel العسير; 74:10 says the Day is غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ for disbelievers. The difficulty shifts from an animal's untrained movement to the final day, extending the root's contrast without equating the scenes.

The section says a rider's ease and the saved person's safety come from a giver beyond themselves. 96:7 describes a person who sees himself as self-sufficient, the opposite stance that makes dependence on a gift visible.
After 69:28 says wealth did not avail, 69:29 says the speaker's authority has vanished. It completes the section's claim that property cannot help at the moment of falling.

The section treats the rider's apparent control as dependence on the One who tamed the mount and leads the saved. 96:6 says the human being transgresses; 96:7 identifies the accompanying illusion of self-sufficiency, a contrary stance to the section's dependence.
The section pictures the God-fearing being led to safety by another. 39:61 says God delivers those who were mindful to their place of triumph, a direct statement of rescue for the God-fearing.

The source-section dictionary phrase جنبت الدابة means leading an animal to one's side. 4:36 uses الْجَارِ الْجُنُبِ for the neighbor at one's side, a different sense of the same root that makes the side relation social rather than equestrian.

The source-section dictionary phrase أعطى البعير means a camel yields; 108:1 uses إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ for God's bestowal. The shared giving form contrasts animal submission with a gift granted by God.

If the oath's العاديات are read as charging horses, 100:1 gives the fast, panting gait opposite the source-section dictionary's horse that moves cautiously to spare a painful hoof. The horse reading is traditional, so this is a specific but interpretive parallel.

On the same horse reading of 100:1, 100:2 continues the rush with sparks struck in the charge; this reverses the source-section's hoof-sensitive horse that avoids painful steps. The verse does not itself name the horse, so the link depends on 100:1's reading.

The section's untrained camel resists being ridden, while the cow in 2:71 is explicitly not subdued for plowing or irrigation. Its different work setting marks the boundary between a tractable mount and an animal not yet made useful for labor.
The section's God-fearing person is taken aside from Hell; 39:71 drives disbelievers toward it. The same externally directed movement ends in the opposite destination.

The source-section dictionary calls a saddle that does not wound a horse وَاقٍ, from the protection root و ق ي. 16:81 describes clothing and armor that protect people from heat and battle; the same protective function shifts from a mount's back to human bodies.

The section recalls the rider thanking God for a mount made serviceable by Him. 45:12 applies that dependence to the sea: ships run by God's command so people may seek His bounty and give thanks, extending the same travel-and-gratitude relation beyond the road.

The source-section roots ي س ر and ع س ر describe the easy-following mount against the untrained camel. In 2:185, ease and difficulty are explicitly contrasted in God's instruction about fasting, repeating that lexical opposition in a different obligation.

The source-section dictionary phrase أعطى البعير uses أعطى for a camel's yielding. 53:34 describes a person who gives a little and then stops, making the same giving form a specific human counterpoint to the mount's yielding.

The section develops the camel as a mount and a road traveled with another's help. 22:27 sends pilgrims toward the Hajj on foot or on lean camels from distant passes, expanding the riding image into a long journey of worship.
